facts: In 1915 New York ran on a coroner system that Blum describes as corrupt and often failing at its job.
Frederic Mors confessed to several poisonings, escaped real punishment and then vanished; the coroner had claimed there was no way to find chloroform in a corpse.
Blum notes that tests for chloroform did exist in 1915, so the claim was false.
In 1918 Charles Norris became New York City first chief medical examiner, replacing the coroner system.
Norris set up his department in Bellevue Hospital recently completed pathology building, with a forensic chemistry laboratory.
Alexander Gettler was his head toxicologist, a dry, quiet, rigorously thorough technician.
One of Gettler first investigations was wood alcohol: his test ground up a piece of tissue and added chemicals that would produce formaldehyde if wood alcohol had been present.
His tests let the office prove that wood alcohol poisoning was rising; the two men advanced many of the methods used to track poisons in the body.
The book follows Norris and Gettler through a series of linked cases, each built around one poison: chloroform, wood alcohol, cyanide and others.
Gettler is described as the city's first toxicologist; Norris as its first scientifically trained medical examiner.
A chapter summary dates the wood alcohol work to 1918-1919 and places a press conference warning about wood alcohol in December 1919.
scene_details: the coroner claim that nothing could be found in a corpse
a piece of tissue ground up and treated with chemicals that make formaldehyde
a laboratory inside Bellevue new pathology building
tension: A poisoner can walk free because an official says the poison cannot be found, when a test for it already exists.
opening_idea: Open on the coroner's flat statement that chloroform cannot be found in a body, and the poisoner who benefited.

lessons.idea: A claim that something cannot be proved often means nobody has done the test; ask for the measurement before accepting it.
lessons.anchor: the coroner's claim about chloroform vs. tests that existed in 1915

reflect_final: Which claim that something cannot be checked or measured in your own work have you simply accepted, and what first test could you try on it this month?

use_cases.situation: A colleague says a problem cannot be measured.
use_cases.move: Say that a coroner once said chloroform could not be found when tests existed, and ask what the simplest check would be.

use_cases.situation: Someone tells you a claim cannot be verified.
use_cases.move: Ask what test would settle it and who could run it.

use_cases.situation: You assume a recurring household cost cannot be tracked.
use_cases.move: Write down the figure for one month before deciding it is unknowable.

pocket_idea: A coroner said chloroform could not be found in a body; a lab with a test proved him wrong. Test the claim before accepting it.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A New York coroner said chloroform could not be found in a corpse, in a year when tests for it existed.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: In 1915 a New York coroner said no one could find chloroform in a corpse and a poisoner escaped. In 1918 Charles Norris became the first chief medical examiner, built a lab in Bellevue and hired toxicologist Alexander Gettler, whose test showed wood alcohol deaths rising.
